analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. prescription drug list prices at the average price charged in six other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would cap U.S. drug list prices at the average of prices in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the U.K., has sat in committee with no hearing, vote, or action since its May 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for drug companies to charge a U.S. list price higher than the average list price for the same drug in six other developed countries. Companies that overcharge would owe a penalty of ten times the difference, charged on every unit sold. It has been stuck in the Senate health committee since it was introduced.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay cash or pay based on a drug's list price — including the uninsured and people with high deductibles — would see the ceiling on what companies can charge drop to roughly the level paid in peer countries. The bill also forces manufacturers to disclose their prices abroad every year, creating a public record of how much more Americans are asked to pay. People whose cost-sharing is calculated off list prices would benefit indirectly.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the U.S. retail list price of every approved drug and biological product at the average list price charged in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom.
Enforces the cap with a civil penalty equal to ten times the gap between the U.S. price and the foreign average, charged on each unit sold, so underpricing the penalty is not cheaper than complying.

Requires manufacturers to report their U.S. and foreign list prices to Health and Human Services annually, with the agency calculating the foreign average each year and issuing rules to implement the cap.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost directly: their U.S. list prices would be capped at foreign levels and violations would trigger per-unit penalties of ten times the overcharge. Some of the revenue loss could show up as less money for research and development on future drugs, and insurers and pharmacy benefit managers could see the rebate pools they negotiate off list prices shrink.

drawbacks.text: The cap applies only to list prices, but most insured Americans do not pay list price — they pay prices built on the confidential rebates that manufacturers give insurers and pharmacy benefit managers. A list-price ceiling might not lower what insured patients actually pay at the pharmacy counter, so the people who most need relief could see little of it.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that hard price caps can have side effects: manufacturers could respond by raising prices in the six reference countries, which would pull the ceiling up, or by delaying or declining to launch new drugs in the United States, since the bill gives them no exemption for newly approved products.

Enforcement depends entirely on foreign price data, which the Secretary must assemble from both manufacturer reports and public filings abroad; errors or gaps in that data would directly determine the legal U.S. price and the size of penalties.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients paying out of pocket, the potential benefit is large and direct: a legally enforceable ceiling near what peer countries pay, with penalties designed to make evasion expensive. The costs are real but mostly fall on one concentrated industry, though a weaker version of the benefit is a fair criticism — because the bill regulates list prices rather than the net prices insured patients actually face, its help could be uneven, and it could nudge companies to raise prices abroad or slow-roll U.S. launches. On balance it is a straightforward pro-patient bill whose main weakness is design, not intent.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2025 and referred to the Senate health committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill on May 5, 2025, joined by Senator Peter Welch as its only cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, since the price cap never advanced and their current U.S. pricing remains untouched. Patients who pay list price continue to pay among the highest prices in the developed world.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers; patients keep paying U.S. prices

for.name: Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap U.S. drug list prices at the average of six other countries' prices.

for.name: Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Bill Cassidy
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since it was referred to his committee.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: The industry has long campaigned against international reference pricing proposals of this kind, which would tie U.S. prices to lower foreign prices.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only support is one Republican sponsor and one Independent cosponsor; neither party has moved it, and no member has publicly opposed it in the record.

industries.note: The bill caps their U.S. list prices at the average of six foreign countries' prices and fines them ten times the difference for every unit sold above it. Because the U.S. is the world's most profitable drug market, this would directly cut the industry's main source of revenue, which is why similar proposals have drawn fierce industry opposition.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: These intermediaries negotiate discounts off list prices and keep a share of the difference. A lower list-price ceiling could shrink the rebate pools they profit from, even as it lowers the baseline prices their members' cost-sharing is calculated from.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the Senate HELP Committee with a single cosponsor rarely receive a hearing, much less a committee vote, and this one has shown no activity since May 2025. Unless drug pricing becomes a priority in the committee's agenda or the bill attracts a broader coalition, it is very likely to die quietly at the end of this Congress without ever reaching the floor.
